newsitem.title: INDIA: India's falling exports a grave concern-trade group.
newsitem.headline: India's falling exports a grave concern-trade group.

text.p: A fall in Indian exports at the start of fiscal 1997/98 is causing grave concern among exporters, and the Indian rupee should be devalued to help reverse the trend, the Federation of Indian Export Organisations (FIEO) said on Thursday.
"It's a very serious situation and it's causing grave concern to exporters," FIEO president Ramu Deora told Reuters.
"Countries like Malaysia, Indonesia and Pakistan have devalued their currencies to boost exports. Why can't India do it?," he said.
Deora said exports plunged 10.8 percent in April 1997 compared to a rise of 13.7 percent in the same month of the previous year.
Official figures released on June 4 put the fall, which analysts said was partly due to an 11-day truck strike, at 10.1 percent.
Exporters had complained that the strike by around 2.2 million truckowners had delayed about $1 billion worth of exports, which are crucial to the health of the Indian economy.
The Economic Times newspaper warned on Thursday that Indian exports could contract by five to six percent in the first quarter of 1997/8.
Indian export growth in 1996/97 was a meagre 4.0 percent compared to a 21.4 percent in the previous year.
Deora said all export goods -- industrial and agricultural and other items like chemicals and gems and jewellery had been hit.
He said representatives of FIEO and various export promotion councils would meet the commerce minister in New Delhi on June 26 to discuss measures to reverse the worsening trend.
"We are going to discuss the recession in international markets and problems faced by exporters at home. Export business is fast becoming risky, unremunerative and unprofitable," Deora said.
Deora said one of the problems was the prohibitive cost of export credit in India, which was as high as 13-18 percent against an average 9.0 percent in competing countries.
Many export houses were losing interest in their business due to the unencouraging attitude of government agencies implementing export policies, he said.

"The Indian exchange rate is unrealistic and unremunerative as far as exports are concerned. The Indian rupee should have been adjusted downwards by at least 10 percent to 38-40 rupees (against the dollar)," he said.
The Indian rupee has been steady at 35.75/85 against the dollar since mid-1996.
Labour unrest in the State Bank of India (SBI) and its branches in western India in the past week has hit exporters in the region, who depend on credit from the bank.
SBI officers, who went on a week-long strike against the suspension of three colleagues on charges of involvement in a financial scandal, on Thursday resumed work.
